causal_agent: Calcium deficiency combined with irregular water uptake
distribution: Worldwide; common in areas with fluctuating soil moisture or low calcium availability

fruit: Dark, sunken lesion at blossom end of fruit
Lesion may enlarge, become leathery, and lead to fruit rot
First visible on young developing fruits, often in clusters
Internal tissues may also be discolored if condition persists
leaves_and_stems: No direct symptoms on leaves or stems; plants often appear healthy aboveground

cause_and_risk_factors: Insufficient calcium uptake by developing fruit
Irregular watering leading to fluctuating soil moisture
Excessive vegetative growth due to over-fertilization, creating imbalance between root capacity and fruit demand
High humidity reducing transpiration and calcium transport

cultural: Maintain even soil moisture during fruiting via controlled watering or drip irrigation
Mulch to retain soil moisture and reduce fluctuations
Provide adequate spacing and prune to ensure good air circulation and reduce relative humidity
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization; side-dress only if needed to maintain moderate growth
Monitor plant vigor to ensure balance between root and shoot development
chemical: Foliar application of calcium nitrate or calcium chloride (1.5 tsp per gallon water + 0.5 tsp surfactant, e.g., CapSil) weekly during fruiting
Apply sprays in the early morning to reduce risk of phytotoxicity
Avoid excessive calcium applications as it may reduce yields or cause foliage injury
preventive_notes: Focus on consistent cultural practices and calcium availability rather than relying solely on foliar sprays
Monitor soil calcium levels prior to planting and amend soils if needed

references: Brubaker, V. 2016. Calcium: It does a plant good. Greenhouse Grower, January.
